URL: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cjly4rv0q3l0o
BBC News — published 23 September 2026 22:01 BST, updated 24 September 2026 08:10 BST

HEADLINE: Blood tests find high levels of cancer-causing "forever chemical" PFOA in residents of Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, near the AGC Chemicals factory.

FACTS (BBC):
- 49 residents volunteered for independent blood testing by Manchester Metropolitan University, paid for by investigative journalists Watershed and Law for Change. Results were given to them on Wednesday 23 September.
- 70% of the 49 had readings that, under US and German guidelines, could leave them at increased risk of adverse health effects. The UK has no recommended acceptable PFAS level in people.
- PFOA has been banned in the UK since 2020 and is classed by the WHO as a Group 1 carcinogen.
- The Environment Agency and Wyre Council have tested the area since 2024 and found elevated PFOA in soil, eggs and locally grown vegetables. Two allotment sites have been closed and are due to be classified as contaminated land; residents within 1km of the factory are advised to peel home-grown fruit and vegetables.
- The factory began operating in the 1950s under ICI making non-stick pan coating; AGC Chemicals took over in 1999 and used PFOA until 2012. Its replacement chemical EEA-NH4 was found in the blood of 10 residents tested.
- AGC Chemicals said earlier this month the factory will close later this year.
- More than 100 residents are considering a group legal action against AGC Chemicals — Leigh Day says it would be the first UK community claim over forever-chemical contamination.
- Possible health effects listed: reduced thyroid function, kidney cancer, testicular cancer, elevated cholesterol, pre-eclampsia, ulcerative colitis.
- Comparison: DuPont and Chemours settled more than 3,500 PFOA lawsuits in West Virginia for $671m (£526m); both denied wrongdoing.

QUOTES:
Sam Hammond, resident: "When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale." / "I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific."
Mario Panteli, resident: "quite emotional, a shock" — "I bought a property, assuming that this is our forever home. I'm going to have to stop my children from going in the garden, front and back. I feel constricted, like I'm in a cage now."
Andrew Molloy, resident in the highest-risk category: "I was half expecting it to be just normal."
Dr David Megson, Manchester Metropolitan University: "To me, it shows something seriously wrong has happened to that community in that area, that the levels were far higher than anything we would have ever expected to see in the general population."
Sarah Moore, partner at Leigh Day: "What we're looking at in Thornton-Cleveleys at the moment might be seen as something of an outlier. My worry is that it's the tip of the iceberg, it's just the beginning."
AGC Chemicals spokesperson: "Since the wider multi-agency investigation is still ongoing and no formal determination of land contamination has been made, we cannot speculate on future outcomes or next steps."
Wyre Borough Council: "We recognise that PFAS is an emerging area of scientific research and will continue to press for updated advice and guidance from expert health agencies on behalf of our communities as further evidence becomes available."

HOUSEHOLD ANGLE: home-grown food safety, property values, PFAS in everyday products.
